messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eileen, a 75-year-old Oceania-born woman who had spent much of her adult life working as an auditor, described how the war had entered her life in the ordinary, humiliating spaces where she had once tried to keep order. During a bombing in the city where she was living as a civilian, she became separated from her husband in the confusion and spent hours moving through damaged streets and crowded shelters, trying to account for people and papers while the smell of sweat, unwashed bodies, dust, and fear clung to the air. She said that when she thinks of it now, the memory comes back “like photographs,” fixed and stark, and yet she cannot find words for what happened in a way that feels adequate; she knows it happened, but the experience sits in her mind as vivid scenes and sensations rather than a story she can tell. The smell of sweat or body odour, even now in a busy room, can throw her back into those images, and moments of feeling happy or relaxed can do the same, because she becomes abruptly aware of how vulnerable she was when she had briefly let herself feel safe. When that smell catches her off guard, the feeling is not only that the war is back but that she should have known better than to relax at all, and it immediately feeds her conviction that she is permanently marked by what happened and that other people can see it on her. Those reminders have fed the thought that others can see what happened to her just by looking at her, as if the terror were written on her face, and she has come to believe that her life is not worth living anymore and that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again. Since then, Eileen has become preoccupied with what the event meant and how it might have been avoided. She goes over and over, in a painstaking and self-reproaching way, why it happened to her and how she might have prevented it, replaying every decision from the day of the attack, every route she took, every delay, and every choice she made while trying to preserve a sense of control. That rumination keeps the scene alive in a vividly visual form: the more she searches for a reason, the more she sees those same photographic fragments, and the more she tries to put the experience into words, the more the images take over. The act of thinking it through has only deepened her sense that something terrible was exposed in her, something others can detect immediately, and it has strengthened her belief that she is changed in a permanent, visible way. That conviction of being permanently altered kept pulling the memory back into focus, as if she had to look at it again and again to confirm the proof of her failure. Each return made the scenes feel more vivid and harder to shake, not less. At night she often lies awake reviewing it all, and the memory of the event is intensified rather than settled by this effort to explain it. She had also learned, without quite naming it, to keep herself busy and to avoid quiet moments so the images would not get a foothold; silence and stillness had become things to outmanoeuvre, not rest in. Her sense of danger has become organized around those appraisals. The memory itself had begun to feel like danger arriving in the present, so that when it broke through she no longer experienced it as something finished and over, but as something still happening in her body. Eileen sits with her back against a wall whenever she can, scanning the room so that no one can come up behind her, and she frequently looks over her shoulder as though someone might be following her. After the image broke through, she found herself thinking that if it could still arrive so sharply, there must be something deeply wrong with her, and that thought made her more certain that she was permanently changed. In the workplace, where she still tries to do bookkeeping and audit-related tasks in a small office, she chooses seats that give her a clear view of the door and avoids being trapped in the middle of a meeting room; the smell of sweat from a crowded corridor or the sudden ease of a calm afternoon can be enough to make her tense, alert, and ready to bolt. Keeping herself positioned that way has brought only brief relief, and it has also convinced her that she cannot manage without constant precautions, which only strengthens her belief that the danger is still there. What frightens her most is that if she relaxes, she will be caught off guard again, and that fear has begun to shape her behavior in risky, almost self-defeating ways, as though she were testing whether danger will find her anyway. Even while she is trying to keep herself safe, her mind stays on guard, and every glance behind her or shift of a chair back toward the wall seems to confirm how unsafe she feels. These strategies, however, have not settled her. The rehearsing of conversations before any interaction has made even simple exchanges feel loaded and unnatural, and she often leaves the encounter more aware of herself than of the other person, more convinced that others can tell something happened to her. Her repeated mental reviews of how it could have been prevented and why it happened to her have not brought relief; they have deepened her hopelessness and made her feel that normal emotions are no longer available to her. Each time the memory returns, she becomes more vigilant, and that vigilance, in turn, pulls the images back into focus, so that the photographs in her mind and the bodily feeling of being watched keep reappearing together. The cycle has narrowed her world and made her husband worry, because she is less able to settle into ordinary conversation, more easily startled by the atmosphere of a room, and increasingly withdrawn from the very moments of feeling safe that once gave her some respite. By the time she sought help, Eileen said she was exhausted by the constant effort of bracing herself, replaying the event, and trying to keep her composure in public. She wanted relief from the sense that her face betrays what happened to her and from the conviction that she will never feel normal again, but she was also afraid that if she stopped checking, stopped replaying, or stopped positioning herself defensively, the memory would flood back with the force of the war zone all over again. Once that sense of danger takes hold, the memory seems to come with it; on those high-alert moments, the photographs in her mind surface fully formed, as if her body is still living inside the bombing and the separation from her husband.
